heading: INT. NIGHT FERRY, UPPER OBSERVATION DECK - NIGHT

units.text: INT. NIGHT FERRY, UPPER OBSERVATION DECK - NIGHT
The Baltic, black and wide.
A string of lights on the far shore.
The deck is nearly empty: a few benches, a coffee kiosk shuttered for the night, a rope swaying in the wind.
LENKA HRUBÝ-ASANTE (30s, trench coat, a battered travel case) stands at the rail, staring at the water.
She grips a ticket stub she has folded and unfolded a hundred times.
Footsteps.
She tenses, then relaxes.
OSKAR BELLWEATHER-NAKAGAWA (30s, wool scarf, a paperback in his coat pocket) sits on the nearest bench and takes out a thermos.
He pours.
Offers her a cup without looking up.
She hesitates.
Takes it.
Their fingers brush.
She jerks her hand back, spilling a drop on the deck.
He smiles at the water.
She does not smile, but her shoulders drop an inch.
They stand and sit like that for a long while.
The ferry's horn sounds, deep and mournful.
A third figure rounds the corner: THEODORA "TEDDY" VANDERMEER-OKOYE (50s, uniform of the ferry crew, clipboard).
She pauses, takes in the scene with a practiced eye, and nods to herself.
She crosses the deck.
He stands.
She waves him down.
She checks Lenka's ticket, stamps it, and hands it back.
She gives Oskar his the same way.
She moves on, humming.
Lenka watches her go.
When the crewwoman has vanished, she turns to Oskar, and the question is in her face before it is in her mouth.
He answers by lifting his own ticket and holding it beside hers.
Same destination.
Same cabin number.
Same night.
She stares.
He shrugs, almost apologetic.
She turns away, laughing despite herself.
He stands, joins her at the rail, and for a while they watch the dark.
She leans, slowly, until her shoulder rests against his.
He does not move.
The ferry horn calls again.
Somewhere beneath them, the engines drum a patient pulse, and the lights of the far shore grow, one by one, closer.
He reaches into his pocket.
Withdraws the paperback.
Opens it to the page marked by a ribbon and hands it to her.
She reads the line he has underlined in pencil, and her hand rises to her mouth.
She hands the book back.
He closes it, slips it away.
Neither speaks.
She takes his hand.
He lets her.
The ferry plows on through the dark, and the sea closes quietly behind it.
She turns her face to him.
He leans in.
The horn sounds a third time, long and low, swallowing everything else.
Theodora, at the end of the deck, looks back once, and lets them have the night.
